hints: Look closely at the cause given in the question: these children are born with no T-lymphocytes because of an inherited gene fault. Ask yourself, which option fixes that missing cell problem at its source?
Remember that all lymphocytes develop from stem cells in bone marrow, and that antibodies, antibiotics and vaccines only help if you already have working lymphocytes to use them.
walkthrough:
**Find the root cause**

Think like a doctor first. The problem is not one infection, it is that the child cannot make any T-lymphocytes at all.

T-lymphocytes are needed for cell-mediated immunity and to activate B-lymphocytes, so without them the child is open to many infections.

**Cure means replace, not just protect**

A cure must give the child the ability to make their own working lymphocytes for life.

Giving something temporary, like ready-made antibodies or antibiotics, will wear off and will not fix the inherited fault.

**Why stem cells work**

Haematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow can divide and differentiate into all blood cells, including healthy T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes.

A stem cell transplant (bone marrow transplant) therefore gives the child a new immune system that can respond to infections on its own, which is a cure for SCID.

options.A: This gives only temporary passive immunity. The transfused antibodies are broken down and not replaced because the child still cannot make their own lymphocytes.
options.B: Correct. Healthy donor stem cells can settle in bone marrow and produce normal T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes, restoring a working immune system.
options.C: Antibiotics kill bacteria only and do not work against viruses, and they do not replace missing lymphocytes, so they treat symptoms but do not cure SCID.
options.D: Vaccines need working T and B lymphocytes to make memory cells and antibodies, so they will not work in a child with no T-lymphocytes and could even be dangerous with live vaccines.
